place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育馆新地板 · 十二月
place.en: Yizhong · the new gym floor · December

setup.zh: 露天场子十投七；新地板上全队围着喊，十投二。手环一百一十二：「它分不清看台和野地。」《养性延命录》长息那一句旁的铅笔字：「临考前夜试之，手犹颤。然下笔矣。」手札：「怕的时候，先吐一口长气。」
setup.en: Seven of ten on the open court; two of ten on the new floor with the team yelling around him. 112 on the band: "It can't tell a stand from the wild." The pencil beside the "long breath" line in the old breathing classic: "Tried it the night before the exam; hand still shook. But the pen came down." And in the journal: "When afraid, first let out one long breath."

recap.zh: 一个人十投七，十一个人围着喊十投二；怕是一脚油门。
recap.en: Seven of ten alone, two of ten with eleven yelling; fear is a foot on the throttle.

en: Seven of ten. Two of ten.

story.zh:
零点六秒，落后一分，两个罚球——全场几百双眼睛等着看的，是一个上场概率百分之一的人的手。

那双手五天前还是准的。十二月十四日冬训摸底，阿禾的本子上只有一行：「沈芒　罚球 十投七。」十二月三日起，他在露天场子上顶着北风一天投两百个：眼镜在篮下捡球，老蔡在线边递球；第五天，食堂后门的红薯钻进了铁丝网，球弹出来，它拿脑袋顶回罚球线，坐下，尾巴摇成了一朵花，等着夸。

阿禾合上本子：「替补席上，你最准。」

他先是高兴，高兴完了，心里「咯噔」一下：替补席上最准，那就是说，要是真到了那一步……他没敢往下想。

十六日，球馆的新地板铺好了。阿禾道：「练罚球。一个人站线上，其余的人，围着喊。」

十一个人又拍手又跺脚。他往线上一站，还没拿到球，耳朵先红了。十个，一个比一个快，连出手前那口气都忘了吐。进了两个。

露天场子上，一个人，十投七；新地板上，十一个人围着喊，十投二。手是同一双手，篮筐一寸也没变。

「差的那五个，」阿禾记完了，「不在手上。」

那天夜里，眼镜出了个主意：「你坐着别动，我们喊，看你的手环。」老蔡凑到他耳朵边上，用尽平生之力，唾沫星子喷了他半边脸：「零号！百分之一！」

沈芒眼皮都没眨。手环上的数，一跳一跳，跳到了一百一十二。

眼镜道：「你一步没跑，心跳得跟爬了五层楼一样。人一怕，身子就一脚油门踩到底——嘴干，手抖，心跳到喉咙口。那是给野地里撞见老虎预备的。它分不清看台和野地。」

十七日，他去了古籍部。葛奶奶从老花镜上头看他：「要比赛了？脸跟纸一样。」

他在桌边坐下，闭上眼，想什么也不想。头一秒，想到了「什么也不想」；第五秒，他已经站在罚球线上了。他「腾」地睁开眼，一身冷汗。

葛奶奶头也不抬：「越不想，越想。我年轻时候也这样。」

他请葛奶奶捧出九月里那一函《养性延命录》，翻到讲吐气的那一页：

「凡行气，以鼻内气，以口吐气，微而引之，名曰长息。」

他罚球出手前吐的那一口，原来有名字。这一句的页边，有一行铅笔批注，字小而急：

「临考前夜试之，手犹颤。然下笔矣。」

手还是抖的，可是笔落下去了。几十年前，有个人跟他一样怕过。他又从门边那一函厚书里抽出手札的头一册，翻到靠后的一页：「十九岁九月初三，崖顶。见一门，门上有字。怕。」底下另起一行：「怕的时候，先吐一口长气。」

一个在崖顶，一个在考场，一个在罚球线上。

十八日夜里，他妈在家长群里发了一条：「明晚七点，学校篮球决赛直播。0号是我儿子。」底下回了三十七个「加油」。沈芒「呜——」地一声，把脑袋蒙进被子里，两条腿在被窝里乱蹬，蹬够了，这才明白，他怕的不光是投不进——是投不进的时候，这么多人正好都在看。

快十二点，他给阿禾发：「要是真到那一步，我投不进，怎么办？」

那头「正在输入」了很久。最后来了一句：「那我就记：投不进。」隔了一会儿，又一句：「记下来的，丢不了。」
story.en:
Zero point six seconds, down by one, two free throws — what hundreds of pairs of eyes in the gym were waiting to see was the hands of someone with a one percent chance of playing.

Five days earlier, those hands had been accurate. On December 14th, at the winter-training baseline test, Ahe's notebook had just one line: "Shen Mang  free throws 7 of 10." Since December 3rd he'd been shooting two hundred a day on the outdoor court into the north wind: Specs rebounding under the basket, Old Cai passing him the ball at the line. On the fifth day, Sweet Potato from the cafeteria's back door squeezed in through the wire fence, and when a ball bounced out, he nosed it back to the free-throw line, sat down, tail wagging like a pinwheel, and waited to be praised.

Ahe closed the notebook: "Of everyone on the bench, you're the most accurate."

At first he was pleased; then his heart gave a lurch: the most accurate on the bench meant that if it really came to that... He didn't dare think any further.

On the 16th, the gym's new floor was finished. Ahe said, "Free-throw practice. One person on the line, everyone else around him, yelling."

Eleven people clapping and stomping. The moment he stepped to the line, before he even had the ball, his ears went red. Ten shots, each one faster than the last; he even forgot to let out his breath before the release. Two went in.

On the outdoor court, alone, seven of ten; on the new floor, with eleven people yelling around him, two of ten. The same pair of hands; the rim hadn't moved an inch.

"The five you're missing," said Ahe, when she'd written it down, "aren't in your hands."

That night Specs had an idea: "You sit still, we yell, and we watch your band." Old Cai leaned in to his ear and shouted with all the strength he had, spraying spit over half his face: "Number Zero! One percent!"

Shen Mang didn't even blink. The number on his fitness band jumped and jumped, up to one hundred and twelve.

Specs said, "You haven't run a single step, and your heart's going like you just climbed five flights of stairs. When people get scared, the body floors the gas — dry mouth, shaking hands, heart in your throat. That's meant for running into a tiger out in the wild. It can't tell the stands from the wild."

On the 17th he went to the Rare Books Room. Granny Ge looked at him over the top of her reading glasses: "Got a game coming up? Your face is as white as paper."

He sat down at a table, closed his eyes, and tried to think of nothing. In the first second, he thought of "nothing"; by the fifth, he was already standing on the free-throw line. His eyes flew open, and he was in a cold sweat.

Granny Ge didn't look up: "The harder you try not to think, the more you think. I was like that when I was young."

He asked Granny Ge to bring out the September case of *Records of Nourishing Nature and Prolonging Life* and turned to the page on breathing out:

"In all circulation of qi, take the breath in through the nose and let it out through the mouth, faintly, drawing it long; this is called the long breath."

So the breath he let out before every free throw had a name. In the margin beside that sentence was a line of pencil, the writing small and hurried:

"Tried it the night before the exam. My hand still shook. But the pen came down."

The hand still shook, but the pen came down. Decades ago, someone had been as scared as he was. He drew the first volume of the journal out of the case of thick books by the door again and turned to a page near the back: "Age nineteen, third day of the ninth month. The clifftop. Saw a door, with writing on it. Afraid." Below, on a new line: "When afraid, first let out one long breath."

One on a clifftop, one in an exam hall, one on the free-throw line.

On the night of the 18th, his mom posted in the parents' group: "Tomorrow at seven, the school basketball final is livestreamed. Number 0 is my son." Below it came thirty-seven "Go for it!"s. Shen Mang let out a "Waaah—", pulled the covers over his head, and kicked his legs wildly under the quilt; when he was done kicking, only then did he understand: what scared him wasn't just missing — it was that when he missed, all these people would be watching.

Near midnight, he messaged Ahe: "If it really comes to that and I miss, what do I do?"

On her end, "typing…" went on for a long time. At last one line came: "Then I'll write down: missed." A while later, another: "What gets written down doesn't get lost."

exits.means: goes to the final on the nineteenth
